newsitem.title: USA: CBOT rice shoots to highs on El Nino watch.
newsitem.headline: CBOT rice shoots to highs on El Nino watch.

text.p: CBOT rice futures this week scooted to a series of contract highs and observers cited an "El Nino watch" as central to the market's performance.
"It's a throw up a red flag thing because of the possibilities but we've seen no problems so far," said Neauman Coleman, Senior Vice President for futures at the Dean Witter office in Memphis, Tenn.

El Nino is a periodic warming of the Pacific Ocean off South America that has profound consequences for global weather. The El Nino weather patterns have in the past caused drought in some Asian nationas and could cut the world rice crop, particularly in India, traders said.
"There has been more than ample media coverage about the El Nino weather pattern but whether it develops or not remains to be seen," Coleman said.
Albert Peterlin, U.S. Agriculture Department's chief meteoroogist, this week suggested caution about drawing conclusions about the effect the El Nino would have on world crops this year.

CBOT new-crop September rice Thursday shot to a contract high of $10.61 per cwt, besting the previous high of $10.44 set Wednesday. Rice futures trading volume also climbed this week from recent "routine" levels of from roughly 200 to 500 lots to a high Thursday of 2,013 contracts. The record high trading volume is 2,775 contracts set Feb 5, 1997.
Trading was more subdued Friday, and September delivery closed one cent lower at $10.45 but deferred January set a contract high early of $10.46 and ended the session at $10.44, up four cents.

"There is no margin for error. Keep an eye on Asian weather. If they have a crop shortfall over there this thing (CBOT rice contract) is going to go nuts," a trader said. "Even under average conditions we're not going to build stocks of high grade rice which is what is traded here."
Long grain rice, the class traded at CBOT, was estimated in early June by the USDA to total 162.5 million cwt in the U.S. for the 1997-98 marketing year (August 1-July 31).

That production forecast was below the 183.2 million cwt produced last year and 1997-98 ending stocks of long grain rice in the U.S. were pegged by USDA at 21.6 million cwt, below the previous year's ending stocks tally at 24.2 million cwt.
U.S. weather this summer has been conducive for rice and grain production although the rice crop this spring was seeded during an unusually cool spell.
But the world weather patterns have come to the forefront of trade thinking.
"The weather is good here but elsewhere there are problems and El Nino could cause a drought in the Southern Hemisphere," said Dean Witter's CBOT floor trader Vic Lespinasse.

Bedford, Massacheutts-based Weather Service Corp Friday cited mostly favorable conditions for early double-crop rice in South China and for single-crop rice in Central China. In Japan and South Korea planting continues but is done in many areas. Planting was slowed by a wet spring but moisture is mostly adequate to surplus for crop development, WSC said.
Scattered showers improved conditions for planting Kharif rice in India. Some areas could still use rain as the Monsoon is still weak, WSC said.
WSC said favorable conditions for development of main season rice in the Philippines and the harvest of main season rice in Java, Indonesia.
